The size of a **matrix**, given as the number of rows by the number of columns (rows × columns).
Multiplying every entry of a **matrix** by a single constant number.

An operation that combines two matrices by multiplying rows of the first by columns of the second, requiring the **matrix dimensions** to be compatible (columns of the first equal rows of the second).
A **matrix** that represents a system of linear equations by combining the coefficient columns with a column of constants.
A single number calculated from a square **matrix** that indicates whether the matrix has an **inverse matrix**.
A **matrix** that, when multiplied by the original matrix, produces the identity matrix; it exists only when the **determinant** is nonzero.

practiceQuestions.question: Add the matrices A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, -1], [0, 2]].
practiceQuestions.explanation: Adding two matrices of the same **matrix dimensions** means adding corresponding entries: [[1+5, 2-1], [3+0, 4+2]] = [[6, 1], [3, 6]].

practiceQuestions.question: Matrix A has dimensions 2×3 and matrix B has dimensions 3×4. What are the dimensions of AB, and is BA defined?
choices: AB is 2×4; BA is not defined
AB is not defined; BA is 4×2
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Matrix multiplication** AB is defined because A's columns (3) match B's rows (3), giving a 2×4 result; BA is undefined because B's columns (4) do not match A's rows (2).

practiceQuestions.question: What is the determinant of [[4, 3], [2, 5]]?
practiceQuestions.explanation: For a 2×2 matrix, the **determinant** is (4)(5) - (3)(2) = 20 - 6 = 14.

practiceQuestions.question: Multiply [[1, 2]] (a 1×2 matrix) by [[3], [4]] (a 2×1 matrix).
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Matrix multiplication** sums the products of corresponding entries: (1)(3) + (2)(4) = 3 + 8 = 11, giving the 1×1 result [11].

practiceQuestions.question: Which augmented matrix correctly represents the system 3x - y = 7 and x + 2y = -4?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **augmented matrix** lists each equation's coefficients and constant in order, so 3x - y = 7 becomes [3, -1, 7] and x + 2y = -4 becomes [1, 2, -4].

lessons.title: Conic Sections: Circles, Parabolas, and Ellipses
lessons.summary: **Conic sections** are curves formed by slicing a cone, and each type has its own standard algebraic form centered at a point (h, k), the **center**. A **circle** follows (x-h)² + (y-k)² = r², where r is the radius, while a **parabola** opens horizontally or vertically depending on which variable is squared. An **ellipse** has two unequal axes, described by (x-h)²/a² + (y-k)²/b² = 1, where the longer axis is the **major axis** and the shorter is the **minor axis**.

keyTerms.definition: A curve, such as a **circle**, **parabola**, or **ellipse**, formed by the intersection of a plane and a cone.
The point (h, k) around which a **circle** or **ellipse** is symmetric.
A **conic section** with equation (x-h)² + (y-k)² = r², where (h,k) is the **center** and r is the radius.
A **conic section** formed by a squared term in only one variable, opening vertically or horizontally.
A **conic section** with equation (x-h)²/a² + (y-k)²/b² = 1, having a **major axis** and a **minor axis** of different lengths.
The longer axis of an **ellipse**, with length 2a where a² is the larger denominator.
The shorter axis of an **ellipse**, with length 2b where b² is the smaller denominator.

practiceQuestions.question: What are the center and radius of the circle (x - 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In the standard form of a **circle**, (h, k) gives the **center** and r² = 25 gives radius r = 5, so the center is (3, -2) and the radius is 5.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the equation of a circle with center (0, 4) and radius 6?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Using the standard form of a **circle** with **center** (0, 4) and radius 6: x² + (y - 4)² = 6² = 36.

practiceQuestions.question: What type of conic section is described by 4x² + 9y² = 36?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dividing by 36 gives x²/9 + y²/4 = 1, where both variables are squared with different, positive denominators, which is the standard form of an **ellipse** (a **circle** would require equal denominators, and a **parabola** would have only one squared variable).

practiceQuestions.question: For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, what is the length of the major axis?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Since 25 is the larger denominator, a² = 25 and a = 5; the **major axis** length is 2a = 10.

practiceQuestions.question: A circular fountain has the equation x² + y² = 49, measured in feet from the center. What is the diameter of the fountain?
practiceQuestions.explanation: This **circle** has r² = 49, so the radius r = 7 feet, and the diameter is twice the radius, or 14 feet.

title: Advanced Chemistry
description: Lab science credit covering atomic structure, bonding, stoichiometry, reactions, gases, solutions, and acid-base chemistry.

lessons.title: Classifying Matter and Measurement
lessons.summary: Chemists classify **matter** into pure substances such as **compounds** and combinations called **mixtures**, including **homogeneous mixtures** where components are evenly distributed. Substances are described using **physical properties**, which can be observed without changing identity, and **chemical properties**, which appear only when a substance reacts to form something new. Careful lab work also depends on **significant figures** to show measurement precision and on derived quantities like **density**, the ratio of mass to volume.

keyTerms.definition: A pure substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, such as water (H2O).
A combination of two or more substances that are only physically combined and can be separated without a chemical reaction.
A type of **mixture** in which the components are evenly distributed throughout, so the mixture looks the same at every point, such as salt water.
A characteristic, such as color or melting point, that can be observed or measured without changing a substance's chemical identity.
A characteristic that describes how a substance reacts with other substances to form new substances.
A physical property equal to an object's mass divided by its volume, usually expressed in g/mL or g/cm3.
The digits in a measurement that are known with certainty plus one estimated digit, showing how precise a measurement is.

practiceQuestions.question: Salt fully dissolved in water forms a solution that looks the same throughout the container. This solution is best classified as a:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Because the dissolved salt is evenly distributed and cannot be seen as separate particles, the salt water is a **homogeneous mixture**, not a **compound**, since the salt and water are only physically combined.

practiceQuestions.question: A mineral sample has a mass of 24.0 g and a volume of 8.0 mL. What is its density?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Density** equals mass divided by volume: 24.0 g ÷ 8.0 mL = 3.0 g/mL.

practiceQuestions.question: A student records a liquid's volume as 12.50 mL using a graduated cylinder. How many significant figures does this measurement contain?
practiceQuestions.explanation: All non-zero digits and the trailing zero after the decimal point are counted, so 12.50 mL has 4 **significant figures**, reflecting the precision of the instrument.

practiceQuestions.question: Iron slowly turning to reddish rust in damp air demonstrates which type of property?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance (iron oxide), so it illustrates a **chemical property** rather than a **physical property**, which would not change the iron's identity.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is a pure substance rather than a mixture?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Distilled water is a **compound** made of a fixed ratio of hydrogen and oxygen, making it a pure substance, unlike the listed **mixtures**, which have variable composition.

lessons.title: Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration
lessons.summary: Atoms are built from a dense **nucleus** containing **protons** and **neutrons**, surrounded by electrons arranged in energy levels. An atom's **atomic number** equals its proton count, while its **mass number** is the sum of protons and neutrons; atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are **isotopes**. **Electron configuration** describes how electrons fill orbitals from lowest to highest energy, which helps explain similarities among elements.

keyTerms.definition: The small, dense center of an atom that contains protons and neutrons and holds almost all of the atom's mass.
A positively charged subatomic particle found in the **nucleus**; the number of protons defines an element's **atomic number**.
An uncharged subatomic particle found in the **nucleus** that adds mass but no electric charge.
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which identifies the element.
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.
An atom of the same element (same **atomic number**) that has a different number of neutrons, and therefore a different **mass number**.
The arrangement of electrons in an atom's energy levels and orbitals, typically filled from lowest to highest energy.

practiceQuestions.question: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. What is its mass number?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **mass number** is the sum of protons and neutrons: 17 + 18 = 35.

practiceQuestions.question: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. These two atoms are best described as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different **mass numbers**, are **isotopes**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which subatomic particle is located in the nucleus and carries no electric charge?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **neutron** resides in the **nucleus** alongside the **proton** but has no charge, while electrons orbit outside the nucleus.

practiceQuestions.question: An element has an atomic number of 12. How many protons and how many electrons does a neutral atom of this element contain?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **atomic number** gives the proton count directly, and a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the correct electron configuration for a neutral sodium atom (atomic number 11)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sodium has 11 electrons, which fill in order of increasing energy as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1, giving the correct **electron configuration**.

lessons.title: Periodic Trends
lessons.summary: The **periodic table** arranges elements by increasing atomic number so that elements with similar properties fall into the same **group** (column). Moving across a **period** (row), **atomic radius** generally decreases while **ionization energy** and **electronegativity** generally increase, because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer to the nucleus.

keyTerms.definition: A chart that organizes elements by increasing atomic number so elements with similar chemical properties line up in the same column.
A vertical column of the periodic table containing elements with similar valence electron arrangements and chemical behavior.
A horizontal row of the periodic table across which atomic number increases by one from element to element.
A measure of the size of an atom, generally decreasing across a **period** and increasing down a **group**.
The energy required to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom; it generally increases across a **period**.
A measure of how strongly an atom attracts shared electrons in a chemical bond; it generally increases across a **period**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which element would you expect to have the largest atomic radius: Li, Na, K, or Rb?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Atomic radius** increases down a **group** as electrons occupy higher energy levels farther from the nucleus, so Rb, lowest in the group, is largest.

practiceQuestions.question: As you move left to right across Period 3 (Na to Ar), ionization energy generally:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Across a **period**, increasing nuclear charge holds electrons more tightly, so **ionization energy** generally increases.

practiceQuestions.question: Fluorine has one of the highest electronegativity values on the periodic table. This means fluorine:
choices: Strongly attracts shared electrons in bonds
Has a very large atomic radius
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Electronegativity** measures an atom's pull on shared electrons, and fluorine's high value means it strongly attracts bonding electrons toward itself.

practiceQuestions.question: A student graphs atomic radius vs. atomic number for Period 2 elements and finds the value decreases steadily from lithium to neon. This trend is best explained by:
choices: Decreasing nuclear charge across the period
Increasing nuclear charge pulling electrons closer across the period
Electrons moving to higher energy levels across the period
practiceQuestions.explanation: Across a **period**, protons are added to the nucleus while electrons fill the same energy level, so increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud inward, shrinking **atomic radius**.

practiceQuestions.question: Elements in the same column of the periodic table, such as Group 1 (alkali metals), share similar chemical behavior mainly because they have the same:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Elements in a **group** share the same number of valence electrons, which produces similar bonding behavior despite differing **atomic radius** values.

lessons.title: Ionic Bonding and Compounds
lessons.summary: **Ionic bonds** form when atoms transfer electrons, creating oppositely charged **ions**, positive **cations** and negative **anions**, that attract each other through electrostatic force. The resulting **ionic compounds** arrange ions in a repeating **crystal lattice**, giving them high melting points and the ability to conduct electricity only when melted or dissolved.

keyTerms.definition: An electrostatic attraction between a positively charged ion and a negatively charged ion, formed when electrons transfer from one atom to another.
An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons, giving it a net electric charge.
A positively charged **ion**, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.
A negatively charged **ion**, formed when an atom gains one or more electrons.
A compound made of **cations** and **anions** held together by **ionic bonds**, typically formed between a metal and a nonmetal.
The repeating, orderly three-dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic solid.

practiceQuestions.question: When a sodium atom reacts with a chlorine atom, sodium transfers an electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes a:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Losing an electron gives sodium a net positive charge, making it a **cation**, while chlorine gains the electron to become an **anion**.

practiceQuestions.question: What holds the ions together in an ionic compound like NaCl?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **ionic bond** is the electrostatic attraction between a **cation** and an **anion**, not a shared electron pair.

practiceQuestions.question: Ionic compounds such as table salt have high melting points mainly because:
choices: Their ions are arranged in a strong, repeating crystal lattice
They have weak van der Waals forces
practiceQuestions.explanation: The strong electrostatic attractions throughout the **crystal lattice** of an **ionic compound** require large amounts of energy to break apart, giving high melting points.

practiceQuestions.question: A solid sample does not conduct electricity, but when melted, the liquid conducts electricity well. This behavior is most consistent with the sample being a(n):
practiceQuestions.explanation: In the solid state, **ions** are locked in a **crystal lattice** and cannot move, but once melted, the ions become mobile and can carry current, a hallmark of **ionic compounds**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which particle is formed when a nonmetal atom gains one or more electrons?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gaining electrons gives an atom a net negative charge, forming an **anion**, the negative counterpart to a **cation**.

lessons.title: Covalent Bonding and Molecular Geometry
lessons.summary: In a **covalent bond**, atoms share pairs of electrons rather than transferring them, forming discrete **molecules**. **Lewis structures** show how valence electrons are arranged as bonding pairs and **lone pairs**, and **VSEPR theory** uses electron pair repulsion to predict a molecule's three-dimensional **molecular geometry**, such as linear, bent, or tetrahedral.

keyTerms.definition: A chemical bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A group of two or more atoms held together by **covalent bonds**.
A diagram that shows the arrangement of valence electrons around atoms in a molecule as bonding pairs and **lone pairs**.
A pair of valence electrons on an atom that is not shared in a **covalent bond**.
A model (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) that predicts **molecular geometry** based on the idea that electron pairs arrange themselves to minimize repulsion.
The three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule, such as linear, bent, trigonal planar, or tetrahedral.

practiceQuestions.question: In a water molecule (H2O), the oxygen atom shares electrons with two hydrogen atoms. This type of bond is called a:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sharing electron pairs between atoms, rather than transferring them, defines a **covalent bond**.

practiceQuestions.question: According to VSEPR theory, why does a water molecule have a bent shape rather than a linear shape?
choices: The two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bonding pairs, pushing the hydrogens closer together
Water has no lone pairs, so it must be linear
Hydrogen atoms repel each other strongly
practiceQuestions.explanation: **VSEPR theory** states that all electron regions, including **lone pairs**, repel each other; oxygen's two lone pairs push the bonding pairs together, producing a bent **molecular geometry**.

practiceQuestions.question: In a correctly drawn Lewis structure for ammonia (NH3), how many lone pairs are on the central nitrogen atom?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons; three are used in bonding pairs with hydrogen, leaving one **lone pair**, as shown in the **Lewis structure**.

practiceQuestions.question: A molecule with four bonding pairs and no lone pairs around its central atom, such as CH4, has which molecular geometry?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Four bonding regions with no **lone pairs** spread as far apart as possible, giving a tetrahedral **molecular geometry**, as predicted by **VSEPR theory**.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of drawing a Lewis structure for a molecule?
choices: To show the isotopic composition of each atom
To show how valence electrons are shared and arranged as bonding and lone pairs
To determine the atomic number of each atom
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **Lewis structure** maps out valence electrons as bonding pairs and **lone pairs**, which is the foundation for predicting shape with **VSEPR theory**.

lessons.title: Intermolecular Forces and Physical Properties
lessons.summary: Beyond the covalent bonds within a molecule, weaker **intermolecular forces** act between molecules and determine properties like boiling point and solubility. These include **london dispersion forces** present in all molecules, **dipole-dipole forces** between polar molecules, and **hydrogen bonding**, an especially strong interaction involving hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F. A molecule's overall **polarity** depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.

keyTerms.definition: An attractive force that acts between separate molecules, weaker than the covalent bonds within a molecule, that influences boiling point, melting point, and solubility.
A weak, temporary **intermolecular force** caused by momentary shifts in electron distribution, present between all molecules.
An **intermolecular force** between polar molecules, where the positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of another.
An unusually strong type of dipole-dipole **intermolecular force** that occurs when hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom (nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine).
A property of a molecule describing the uneven distribution of electron density, resulting in partial positive and negative regions.

practiceQuestions.question: Water has an unusually high boiling point for its small size mainly because of:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Water's H atoms bonded to a highly electronegative O atom allow strong **hydrogen bonding**, a powerful type of **intermolecular force** that raises boiling point.

practiceQuestions.question: Which type of intermolecular force is present between all molecules, polar or nonpolar?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **London dispersion forces** arise from temporary electron shifts and occur in every molecule, unlike **dipole-dipole forces**, which require permanent **polarity**.

practiceQuestions.question: Two molecules of similar size and mass are compared: one is nonpolar and one is slightly polar. The polar molecule has a higher boiling point. This is best explained by:
choices: The polar molecule has stronger dipole-dipole forces in addition to london dispersion forces
The nonpolar molecule has hydrogen bonding
The polar molecule has ionic bonds
Boiling point does not depend on intermolecular forces
practiceQuestions.explanation: A polar molecule experiences both **london dispersion forces** and additional **dipole-dipole forces**, increasing the total **intermolecular force** strength and raising boiling point.

practiceQuestions.question: CO2 is a nonpolar molecule even though each C=O bond is polar. This is because:
choices: CO2 has no lone pairs anywhere in the molecule
CO2's linear, symmetric shape causes the two bond dipoles to cancel
Carbon and oxygen have identical electronegativity
CO2 has hydrogen bonding that cancels polarity
practiceQuestions.explanation: Even with polar bonds, a symmetric linear shape causes the individual bond dipoles to cancel, giving the molecule overall zero net **polarity**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following molecules would you expect to exhibit hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Hydrogen bonding** requires hydrogen bonded directly to N, O, or F; ammonia (NH3) meets this requirement, unlike the other nonpolar or non-qualifying molecules.

lessons.title: Naming Compounds: Ionic and Covalent Nomenclature
lessons.summary: **Chemical nomenclature** is the system of rules for naming compounds so their formula can be determined from the name alone, and vice versa. For binary ionic compounds, the cation is named first followed by the anion with an **-ide** suffix (sodium chloride, NaCl). Transition metals that form more than one charge require the **Stock system**, a Roman numeral showing the cation's charge (iron(III) oxide). Compounds containing a **polyatomic ion**, like sulfate (SO4^2-) or nitrate (NO3-), keep that ion's name as a unit. Covalent compounds between two nonmetals instead use **Greek prefixes** (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-) to show exactly how many atoms of each element are present, since covalent compounds don't follow fixed ionic charge ratios.

keyTerms.definition: The systematic set of rules used to name chemical compounds based on their composition.
A compound made of exactly two elements, one a metal cation and one a nonmetal anion, named cation-first with an -ide suffix on the anion.
A Roman numeral placed after a transition metal's name to show its charge in that compound, used because many transition metals form more than one possible cation.
A charged group of covalently bonded atoms (such as sulfate, SO4^2-, or nitrate, NO3-) that acts as a single unit in ionic compounds and keeps its own name.
Prefixes (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, etc.) used to name covalent compounds, showing exactly how many atoms of each element are present.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the correct name for NaCl?
practiceQuestions.explanation: For a **binary ionic compound**, the cation name (sodium) is followed by the anion with an -ide suffix (chloride) — no prefix or Roman numeral is needed since sodium only forms a +1 ion.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does iron(III) oxide need a Roman numeral in its name, but sodium chloride does not?
choices: Iron is a nonmetal and sodium is a metal
Iron is a transition metal that can form more than one possible charge, so the Stock system specifies which one
Oxide compounds always require Roman numerals
Roman numerals are only used for covalent compounds
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **Stock system** Roman numeral is needed for transition metals like iron, which can form multiple charges (Fe^2+ or Fe^3+) — sodium only ever forms Na+, so no numeral is needed.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the correct name for CaSO4?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sulfate (SO4^2-) is a **polyatomic ion** that keeps its own name as a unit, so the compound is simply calcium sulfate.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the correct name for N2O4?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Since this is a covalent compound between two nonmetals, **Greek prefixes** show the exact atom counts: di- for two nitrogen atoms and tetr(a)- for four oxygen atoms.

practiceQuestions.question: Why do covalent compound names use Greek prefixes (like di- and tri-) while ionic compound names do not?
choices: Covalent compounds are always larger than ionic compounds
Ionic compound ratios are fixed by charge balance and can be determined without stating atom counts, while covalent compounds need prefixes to show their exact atom ratio
Greek prefixes are only used for compounds containing oxygen
Ionic compounds never contain more than one atom of any element
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ionic formulas are determined by balancing charges, so the ratio is implied by the ions' names, but covalent compounds can form in several different atom ratios, so **Greek prefixes** are needed to specify which one.

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions and Balancing Equations
lessons.summary: A **chemical reaction** rearranges atoms from **reactants** into new **products**, and the **law of conservation of mass** requires that atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so **chemical equations** must be **balanced equations** with equal numbers of each atom on both sides. Reactions can be classified into types such as **synthesis reactions**, **decomposition reactions**, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion.

keyTerms.definition: A process in which reactants are transformed into new products through the breaking and forming of chemical bonds.
A starting substance that is consumed in a **chemical reaction**.
A new substance formed as a result of a **chemical reaction**.
The principle that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.
A chemical equation in which the same number of atoms of each element appears on both the reactant and product sides.
A reaction in which two or more simple substances combine to form one more complex product.
A reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler products.

practiceQuestions.question: Which coefficient set correctly balances the equation: __H2 + __O2 → __H2O?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O gives 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms on each side, satisfying the **law of conservation of mass** in a **balanced equation**.

practiceQuestions.question: In the reaction 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, which substances are the reactants?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Reactants** are the starting substances consumed in a **chemical reaction**; here Mg and O2 combine to form the **product** MgO.

practiceQuestions.question: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
choices: To make the equation easier to read
To satisfy the law of conservation of mass by keeping equal atoms on both sides
To ensure all reactants are gases
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **law of conservation of mass** requires that atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so a **balanced equation** must show equal atoms of each element on both sides.

practiceQuestions.question: The reaction 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2, where one compound breaks down into simpler products, is classified as a:
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **decomposition reaction** occurs when a single compound breaks apart into two or more simpler **products**, as hydrogen peroxide does here.

practiceQuestions.question: The reaction N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, where two simple substances combine into one compound, is an example of a:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Combining two or more simple **reactants** into a single, more complex **product** defines a **synthesis reaction**.

lessons.title: The Mole and Stoichiometric Calculations
lessons.summary: The **mole** is chemistry's counting unit, where one mole of any substance contains **Avogadro's number** (6.022 × 10^23) of particles, and a substance's **molar mass** (in g/mol) allows conversion between grams and moles. **Stoichiometry** uses the balanced equation's **mole ratio** to calculate how much product forms or how much reactant is needed.

keyTerms.definition: The SI unit for amount of substance, equal to **Avogadro's number** (6.022 × 10^23) of particles of that substance.
The number of particles in one **mole** of a substance, approximately 6.022 × 10^23.
The mass in grams of one **mole** of a substance, numerically equal to its atomic or molecular mass in atomic mass units.
The calculation of quantitative relationships between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation, using **mole ratios**.
The ratio between moles of two substances in a balanced chemical equation, taken from their coefficients.

practiceQuestions.question: How many molecules are in 2.0 moles of CO2?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Multiplying moles by **Avogadro's number** gives 2.0 mol × 6.022 × 10^23/mol ≈ 1.2 × 10^24 molecules.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the molar mass of water, H2O? (H = 1.0 g/mol, O = 16.0 g/mol)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Adding the atomic masses, 2(1.0) + 16.0 = 18.0 g/mol, gives water's **molar mass**.

practiceQuestions.question: How many moles are in 36.0 g of water (molar mass 18.0 g/mol)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dividing mass by **molar mass**, 36.0 g ÷ 18.0 g/mol = 2.0 mol.

practiceQuestions.question: For the reaction N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, how many moles of NH3 are produced from 6.0 moles of H2, assuming excess N2?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Using the **mole ratio** of 2 mol NH3 to 3 mol H2 from the balanced equation, 6.0 mol H2 × (2 mol NH3 / 3 mol H2) = 4.0 mol NH3, an application of **stoichiometry**.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is the mole considered chemistry's essential counting unit?
choices: It lets chemists convert between the invisibly small scale of atoms and molecules and the measurable scale of grams using Avogadro's number
It replaces the need for balanced equations
It measures temperature changes during reactions
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **mole**, linked to **Avogadro's number**, bridges the atomic scale and the measurable gram scale, making **stoichiometry** calculations possible.

lessons.title: Limiting Reactants and Percent Yield
lessons.summary: In many reactions, one reactant runs out first and stops the reaction; this is the **limiting reactant**, while the leftover reactant is the **excess reactant**. The amount of product calculated from the limiting reactant is the **theoretical yield**, while the amount actually collected in the lab is the **actual yield**; comparing them gives the **percent yield**, a measure of a reaction's efficiency.

keyTerms.definition: The reactant that is completely used up first in a chemical reaction, determining the maximum amount of product that can form.
A reactant that remains unreacted after the **limiting reactant** is used up.
The maximum amount of product predicted from stoichiometric calculations, based on the **limiting reactant**.
The amount of product actually obtained from carrying out a reaction in the lab.
The ratio of **actual yield** to **theoretical yield**, expressed as a percentage, showing how efficient a reaction was.

practiceQuestions.question: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, if 4 mol H2 and 1 mol O2 are combined, which reactant is limiting?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The ratio requires 2 mol H2 per 1 mol O2; with 4 mol H2 present, only 2 mol would be needed for 1 mol O2, leaving H2 as the **excess reactant** and O2 as the **limiting reactant**.

practiceQuestions.question: A reaction's stoichiometric calculations predict 20.0 g of product should form. This predicted amount is called the:
practiceQuestions.explanation: The amount calculated from the **limiting reactant** using stoichiometry is the **theoretical yield**.

practiceQuestions.question: A student's theoretical yield for a reaction is 20.0 g, but only 16.0 g of product is actually collected. What is the percent yield?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Percent yield** = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100% = (16.0 g ÷ 20.0 g) × 100% = 80%.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is percent yield in a real lab experiment usually less than 100%?
choices: Because the theoretical yield is always miscalculated
Because side reactions, spills, and incomplete reactions cause some product to be lost
Because the limiting reactant is always in excess
Because actual yield is always greater than theoretical yield
practiceQuestions.explanation: Real reactions lose some product to side reactions, transfer losses, or incomplete reactions, so the **actual yield** is typically less than the **theoretical yield**, giving a **percent yield** below 100%.

practiceQuestions.question: Once the limiting reactant is completely consumed in a reaction, what happens to any leftover excess reactant?
choices: It continues to react and produce more product
It remains unreacted because there is no more limiting reactant to combine with
It becomes the new limiting reactant
practiceQuestions.explanation: Once the **limiting reactant** runs out, the reaction stops, leaving the **excess reactant** unreacted.

lessons.title: Gas Laws
lessons.summary: Gas behavior is described by relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and moles. **Boyle's Law** relates pressure and volume at constant temperature, **Charles's Law** relates volume and temperature at constant pressure, and the **combined gas law** merges these relationships. The **ideal gas law** (PV = nRT) connects pressure, volume, moles, and temperature in a single equation, often compared to conditions at **STP**.

keyTerms.definition: At constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a fixed amount of gas are inversely proportional (P1V1 = P2V2).
At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed amount of gas is directly proportional to its absolute (Kelvin) temperature (V1/T1 = V2/T2).
A relationship that merges **Boyle's Law** and **Charles's Law**, relating pressure, volume, and temperature for a fixed amount of gas (P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2).
An equation, PV = nRT, relating a gas's pressure, volume, moles, and temperature using the gas constant R.
Standard temperature and pressure, defined as 0°C (273 K) and 1 atm, a common reference condition for gases.

practiceQuestions.question: A gas occupies 4.0 L at 2.0 atm. If the pressure increases to 4.0 atm at constant temperature, what is the new volume?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Boyle's Law** states P1V1 = P2V2, so (2.0 atm)(4.0 L) = (4.0 atm)(V2), giving V2 = 2.0 L.

practiceQuestions.question: A gas has a volume of 3.0 L at 300 K. If it is heated to 600 K at constant pressure, what is its new volume?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Charles's Law** states V1/T1 = V2/T2, so V2 = (3.0 L)(600 K)/(300 K) = 6.0 L.

practiceQuestions.question: How many moles of gas are present in a 10.0 L container at 2.0 atm and 300 K? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Using the **ideal gas law**, n = PV/RT = (2.0 atm × 10.0 L) / (0.0821 L·atm/mol·K × 300 K) ≈ 0.81 mol.

practiceQuestions.question: A gas sample is described as being at standard temperature and pressure. This means the conditions are:
practiceQuestions.explanation: **STP** is defined as 0°C (273 K) and 1 atm, a standard reference point for comparing gas volumes.

practiceQuestions.question: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. Its volume cannot change, but the pressure increases. Which relationship is being demonstrated?
choices: Boyle's Law, because pressure and volume are inversely related
Charles's Law, because volume and temperature are directly related
The combined gas law, which reduces to a pressure-temperature relationship when volume is held constant
The ideal gas law only applies to liquids, not gases
practiceQuestions.explanation: When volume is held constant, the **combined gas law** (P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2) simplifies to a direct relationship between pressure and temperature.

lessons.title: Solutions and Concentration
lessons.summary: A **solution** is a homogeneous mixture of a **solute** dissolved in a **solvent**. **Molarity** expresses concentration as moles of solute per liter of solution, and **dilution** uses the relationship M1V1 = M2V2 to calculate how a concentrated solution is diluted to a new concentration. **Solubility** describes the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a solvent at a given temperature.

keyTerms.definition: A homogeneous mixture in which a **solute** is uniformly dissolved in a **solvent**.
The substance present in a smaller amount that is dissolved in a **solution**.
The substance present in a larger amount that dissolves the **solute** in a **solution**.
A concentration unit equal to the number of moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L).
The process of adding more solvent to a solution to decrease its concentration, following M1V1 = M2V2.
The maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature.

practiceQuestions.question: In a cup of sweetened tea, the sugar that dissolves is the:
practiceQuestions.explanation: The substance present in the smaller amount and dissolved into the tea is the **solute**, while the water is the **solvent**.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 2.0 mol of NaCl in enough water to make 4.0 L of solution?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Molarity** = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution = 2.0 mol ÷ 4.0 L = 0.50 M.

practiceQuestions.question: A stock solution has a molarity of 6.0 M. How many mL of this stock are needed to prepare 500.0 mL of a 1.5 M solution?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Using the **dilution** equation M1V1 = M2V2: (6.0 M)(V1) = (1.5 M)(500.0 mL), so V1 = 125 mL.

practiceQuestions.question: At 20°C, a solution contains the maximum amount of dissolved salt possible at that temperature, with excess undissolved salt visible on the bottom of the beaker. This solution is best described as:
choices: Saturated, at the solubility limit for that temperature
practiceQuestions.explanation: When a **solution** holds the maximum solute possible for a given temperature, its **solubility** limit, and excess remains undissolved, the solution is saturated.

practiceQuestions.question: For most solid solutes, how does solubility in water typically change as temperature increases?
practiceQuestions.explanation: For most solid solutes, **solubility** in a **solvent** generally increases with rising temperature, allowing more solute to dissolve.

lessons.title: Colligative Properties
lessons.summary: **Colligative properties** are properties of a solution that depend on the number of dissolved **solute particles** rather than their identity. Adding solute causes **boiling point elevation**, which raises boiling point, and **freezing point depression**, which lowers freezing point, compared to the pure solvent. These effects explain practical uses, such as salting icy roads to lower the freezing point of water.

keyTerms.definition: A property of a solution, such as boiling point or freezing point, that depends on the number of dissolved **solute particles** rather than the solute's identity.
The increase in a solvent's boiling point caused by dissolving a solute in it, a **colligative property**.
The decrease in a solvent's freezing point caused by dissolving a solute in it, a **colligative property**.
An individual dissolved particle (molecule or ion) of solute in a solution, whose count determines the size of a colligative effect.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does adding salt to water raise its boiling point?
choices: The dissolved solute particles interfere with the solvent's ability to escape into vapor, requiring more energy to boil
Salt makes water molecules move faster automatically
Salt reacts chemically with water to form a new solvent
Boiling point is unrelated to dissolved particles
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dissolved **solute particles** disrupt the solvent's vaporization, producing **boiling point elevation**, a type of **colligative property**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is a practical application of freezing point depression?
choices: Boiling water faster at high altitude
Spreading salt on icy roads to melt ice at lower temperatures
Cooling a drink with ice cubes
practiceQuestions.explanation: Road salt lowers the freezing point of water through **freezing point depression**, allowing ice to melt below 0°C.

practiceQuestions.question: A solution of 1 mol of NaCl in water produces a greater freezing point depression than a solution of 1 mol of sugar (glucose) in the same amount of water. Why?
choices: NaCl dissociates into two ions in solution, doubling the number of solute particles compared to glucose, which does not dissociate
Sugar has a higher molar mass than salt
NaCl is a covalent compound with stronger bonds
Sugar always freezes water faster than salt
practiceQuestions.explanation: Because a **colligative property** depends on the total number of **solute particles**, and NaCl dissociates into two ions per formula unit while glucose does not, NaCl produces a greater **freezing point depression** for the same molar amount.

practiceQuestions.question: Which property below is classified as a colligative property?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Boiling point elevation** depends only on the number of dissolved **solute particles**, making it a true **colligative property**, unlike color or reactivity.

practiceQuestions.question: A student compares two solutions with the same solvent: Solution A has more total dissolved solute particles than Solution B. Which solution should show a lower freezing point?
choices: Solution A, because more solute particles cause greater freezing point depression
Solution B, because fewer particles cause greater freezing point depression
Both will have the same freezing point
Freezing point does not depend on particle count
practiceQuestions.explanation: Since **freezing point depression** increases with the number of **solute particles**, Solution A, with more dissolved particles, will have the lower freezing point, consistent with the definition of a **colligative property**.

lessons.title: Acids and Bases
lessons.summary: **Acids** release **hydrogen ions** (H+) in water and taste sour, while **bases** release hydroxide ions (OH-) or accept H+ and feel slippery. The **pH scale** measures how acidic or basic a solution is, ranging from 0 (strongly acidic) to 14 (strongly basic), with 7 being neutral. In a **neutralization reaction**, an acid and a base react to form water and a salt.

keyTerms.definition: A substance that releases **hydrogen ions** (H+) when dissolved in water, producing a sour taste and a pH below 7.
A substance that releases hydroxide ions (OH-) or accepts **hydrogen ions** when dissolved in water, producing a pH above 7.
A logarithmic scale from 0 to 14 used to measure how acidic or basic a solution is, with 7 being neutral.
A reaction between an **acid** and a **base** that produces water and a salt.
A positively charged hydrogen particle (H+) whose concentration in solution determines acidity.

practiceQuestions.question: A solution has a pH of 3. This solution is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: On the **pH scale**, values below 7 indicate an **acid**, and a pH of 3 is clearly acidic.

practiceQuestions.question: What ion do bases release or accept in water that raises a solution's pH above 7?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **base** releases hydroxide ions (OH-) or accepts **hydrogen ions**, raising pH above 7 on the **pH scale**.

practiceQuestions.question: When hydrochloric acid (HCl) reacts with sodium hydroxide (NaOH), the products are water and sodium chloride. This is an example of a:
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **acid** reacting with a **base** to form water and a salt is a **neutralization reaction**.

practiceQuestions.question: A student tests two unknown solutions. Solution X turns litmus paper red, while Solution Y turns litmus paper blue. Which best describes X and Y?
choices: X is a base, Y is an acid
X is an acid, Y is a base
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Acids** turn litmus paper red due to their high **hydrogen ion** concentration, while **bases** turn it blue.

practiceQuestions.question: A solution with a pH of 7, such as pure water, is considered:
practiceQuestions.explanation: A pH of exactly 7 on the **pH scale** indicates a neutral solution, with equal concentrations of H+ and OH- ions.

lessons.title: Thermochemistry
lessons.summary: **Thermochemistry** studies the heat energy absorbed or released during chemical and physical changes. An **exothermic reaction** releases heat to its surroundings (negative ΔH), while an **endothermic reaction** absorbs heat from its surroundings (positive ΔH). **Enthalpy** (H) represents the heat content of a system, and **specific heat** describes how much energy is needed to change a substance's temperature.

keyTerms.definition: The branch of chemistry that studies the heat energy absorbed or released during chemical reactions and physical changes.
A reaction that releases heat energy to its surroundings, resulting in a negative change in **enthalpy** (ΔH < 0).
A reaction that absorbs heat energy from its surroundings, resulting in a positive change in **enthalpy** (ΔH > 0).
A measure of the total heat content of a system, often tracked as a change (ΔH) during a reaction.
The amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius.

practiceQuestions.question: A reaction flask feels noticeably warmer to the touch as the reaction proceeds. This reaction is most likely:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Heat released to the surroundings, warming the flask, is characteristic of an **exothermic reaction**, which has a negative change in **enthalpy**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sign of ΔH corresponds to an endothermic reaction?
choices: ΔH is positive, heat is absorbed
ΔH is negative, heat is absorbed
ΔH is positive, heat is released
ΔH is negative, heat is released
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **endothermic reaction** absorbs heat from its surroundings, giving a positive change in **enthalpy**.

practiceQuestions.question: How much heat, in joules, is needed to raise the temperature of 50.0 g of water by 10.0°C? (specific heat of water = 4.18 J/(g·°C))
practiceQuestions.explanation: Using q = m × c × ΔT with **specific heat**: q = (50.0 g)(4.18 J/g·°C)(10.0°C) = 2090 J.

practiceQuestions.question: Melting ice absorbs energy from its surroundings, which is why melting ice cools a drink. This process is best classified as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Because melting ice takes in heat from the surrounding drink, it is an **endothermic reaction**-like process, consistent with the study of **thermochemistry**.

practiceQuestions.question: A substance with a very high specific heat, such as water, will:
choices: Change temperature quickly for a small amount of added heat
Require a large amount of heat energy to change its temperature significantly
Always release heat rather than absorb it
practiceQuestions.explanation: A high **specific heat** means a substance requires more heat energy per gram to change temperature, a key idea in **thermochemistry**.

lessons.title: Reaction Rates and Equilibrium
lessons.summary: **Reaction rate** measures how quickly reactants turn into products, and **collision theory** explains that reactions occur when particles collide with enough energy, called **activation energy**, and proper orientation. Rates increase with higher temperature, concentration, surface area, or the presence of a **catalyst**. Many reactions reach **chemical equilibrium**, a dynamic state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and concentrations remain constant.

keyTerms.definition: The speed at which reactants are converted into products in a chemical reaction, often measured as a change in concentration over time.
The idea that a chemical reaction occurs when reactant particles collide with sufficient energy and correct orientation.
The minimum amount of energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
A substance that increases a reaction's rate by lowering its **activation energy** without being consumed in the reaction.
A dynamic state in a reversible reaction where the forward and reverse **reaction rates** are equal, so concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

practiceQuestions.question: According to collision theory, why does increasing temperature usually increase a reaction's rate?
choices: Particles move slower and collide less often
Particles move faster, colliding more often and more frequently exceeding the activation energy
Temperature has no effect on particle motion
Higher temperature removes the need for activation energy
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Collision theory** explains that raising temperature increases particle speed, so collisions happen more often and more frequently exceed the **activation energy** needed to react.

practiceQuestions.question: A catalyst speeds up a reaction primarily by:
choices: Lowering the activation energy needed for the reaction to occur
Being consumed and becoming part of the product
Increasing the temperature of the reaction mixture
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **catalyst** provides an alternate reaction pathway with lower **activation energy**, speeding up the **reaction rate** without being used up.

practiceQuestions.question: In a reversible reaction, a student observes that the concentrations of reactants and products no longer change over time, even though the reaction is still occurring in both directions. This state is called:
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Chemical equilibrium** is a dynamic state where forward and reverse **reaction rates** are equal, keeping concentrations constant even though the reaction continues.

practiceQuestions.question: Crushing a solid reactant into a fine powder before a reaction typically increases the reaction rate because it:
choices: Decreases the activation energy to zero
Increases the surface area available for collisions between particles
Removes the need for proper collision orientation
Decreases the concentration of the reactant
practiceQuestions.explanation: More surface area allows more particle collisions to occur, increasing the **reaction rate**, consistent with **collision theory**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following best describes activation energy?
choices: The total energy released by an exothermic reaction
The minimum energy needed for colliding particles to react successfully
The energy needed to melt a solid catalyst
The energy stored in chemical equilibrium
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Activation energy** is the minimum energy threshold that reacting particles must reach during a collision, a central idea of **collision theory**.

title: TCC Spanish I & II
stateCourseStandard: TCC SPAN 1411 (fall) + TCC SPAN 1412 (spring), embedded MISD instructor
description: Both semesters of the LOTE sequence, taken in the same school year, completing the state's 2-credit LOTE requirement via TCC dual credit.

lessons.title: Greetings, Introductions, and Courtesy
lessons.summary: Spanish speakers choose greetings based on the time of day and the level of formality a relationship calls for. This lesson reviews essential greetings, farewells, and courtesy expressions, and introduces the crucial distinction between the informal **tú** and formal **usted** forms of "you." Getting formality right is considered a sign of respect throughout the Spanish-speaking world, more so than in casual American English.

keyTerms.definition: "Good morning," used from sunrise until roughly midday.
"Good afternoon," used from midday until dusk.
"Good evening" AND "good night" — the same phrase covers both a greeting and a farewell after dark.
Informal "you," used with friends, family, and peers your own age. Don't confuse with **usted**, the formal version — mixing them up can sound rude to an elder or too stiff with a friend.

Formal "you," used with strangers, elders, teachers, and in professional settings. It is conjugated like "he/she," which trips up beginners who expect a distinct "you" ending — don't confuse it with the informal **tú**.
"Nice to meet you," said only the first time you meet someone — not a repeated greeting like "hello."
"My name is..." / "His/her name is..." — literally "I call myself," not a direct verb "to be named."
Please / thank you / you're welcome — "de nada" literally means "of nothing."

practiceQuestions.question: You are meeting your new teacher for the first time. Which form of "you" should you use with them?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Teachers and other authority figures call for the formal usted, not the informal tú.

practiceQuestions.question: Which greeting is most appropriate at 4:00 in the afternoon?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Buenas tardes covers the period from midday until dusk.

practiceQuestions.question: When is it appropriate to say "Mucho gusto"?
choices: Every time you say hello to someone
Only when meeting someone for the first time
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mucho gusto marks a first introduction, unlike an everyday greeting you repeat.

practiceQuestions.question: Which is the correctly formal way to ask an elderly stranger for the time?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An elderly stranger calls for the formal usted, not tú.

practiceQuestions.question: What does "de nada" mean?
practiceQuestions.explanation: De nada literally means "of nothing" and functions as "you're welcome."

lessons.title: Numbers, Time, and the Classroom
lessons.summary: Numbers, dates, and time expressions are foundational for scheduling and everyday classroom interaction. This lesson also tackles three Spanish words that sound identical but mean very different things — **hay**, **ahí**, and **ay** — and shows how telling time switches between "es" and "son" depending on the hour.

keyTerms.definition: "There is / there are," an invariable form of haber used to state existence (Hay veinte estudiantes). Often confused with **ahí** (a location) and **ay** (an exclamation) because all three are pronounced the same.
"There" (a location), e.g., "El libro está ahí." Don't confuse with **hay** — ahí points to a place, hay states that something exists.
An exclamation like "ouch!" or "oh no!" Don't confuse with **hay**; they sound identical but ay carries no meaning of existence.
"What time is it?"

keyTerms.term: Es la una / Son las dos
keyTerms.definition: "It's one o'clock" / "It's two o'clock" — singular "es" is used only for 1:00, while "son" is used for every other hour.
The date; written day-month-year in Spanish-speaking countries, the opposite of the common U.S. month-day-year order.

keyTerms.term: el cuaderno / la mochila / el lápiz
keyTerms.definition: Notebook / backpack / pencil — basic classroom vocabulary.
Cardinal numbers; 16-29 combine into one word (veintiuno), while 31 and up use "y" (treinta y uno).

practiceQuestions.question: "___ treinta estudiantes en la clase." (There are thirty students in the class.)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hay states existence — "there are."

practiceQuestions.question: "El profesor está ___." (The teacher is over there.)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ahí refers to a location, "there," unlike hay which states existence.

practiceQuestions.question: You just stubbed your toe. What would you exclaim?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ay is the exclamation of pain or surprise, distinct from hay and ahí despite sounding the same.

practiceQuestions.question: How do you say "It's one o'clock"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only 1:00 uses the singular "es"; all other hours use "son."

practiceQuestions.question: In Spanish-speaking countries, la fecha is typically written in what order?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Spanish-speaking countries generally write dates day-month-year, unlike the U.S. convention.

lessons.title: Question Words, Pronouns, and Sentence Structure
lessons.summary: Spanish sentence structure resembles English but has quirks that don't map cleanly onto it: adjectives usually follow the noun, subjects are often dropped because the verb ending shows who's acting, and — perhaps most surprising to English speakers — **double negatives are grammatically required**, not an error.

keyTerms.term: yo, tú, él/ella, nosotros/as, vosotros/as, ellos/ellas
keyTerms.definition: Subject pronouns; vosotros/as is used only in Spain and is replaced by "ustedes" in Latin America.
Because verb endings indicate the subject, Spanish often omits pronouns entirely ("Hablo español" needs no "yo").
Question words: what/who/where/when/why/how; all carry a written accent when used in questions.
Adjectives typically follow the noun they describe ("el libro rojo," not "el rojo libro"), the reverse of standard English order.

Spanish requires stacking negative words for correct grammar: "No veo a nadie" (literally "I don't see nobody") is grammatically correct Spanish, unlike in standard English, where a double negative is considered an error.
Nothing / nobody / never — the negative words commonly stacked together with "no."
Spanish uses an upside-down question mark at the start of a question as well as a normal one at the end.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sentence correctly follows Spanish adjective placement?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Descriptive adjectives typically follow the noun in Spanish.

practiceQuestions.question: Which pronoun would you use in Spain but generally NOT in Latin America?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Vosotros is used in Spain; Latin America uses ustedes for the same meaning.

practiceQuestions.question: Why can Spanish often drop the subject pronoun?
choices: Because the verb ending already shows who is acting
Because it's only used in questions
practiceQuestions.explanation: The verb ending (sujeto tácito) carries the subject information, so the pronoun becomes optional.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sentence demonstrates a grammatically correct Spanish double negative?
practiceQuestions.explanation: "No veo nada" stacks no + nada correctly and is standard, correct Spanish grammar.

practiceQuestions.question: Which question word means "why"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: ¿Por qué? means "why," distinct from ¿cómo? (how), ¿cuándo? (when), and ¿dónde? (where).

lessons.title: Regular Present-Tense Verbs (-ar, -er, -ir)
lessons.summary: Spanish verbs fall into three families based on their infinitive ending: **-ar**, **-er**, and **-ir**. Each family has its own set of six endings attached to the verb stem. This lesson also introduces the **personal a**, a required word with no English equivalent that appears before a specific person or pet used as a direct object.

keyTerms.definition: Conjugation pattern: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan.
Conjugation pattern: como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen.
Conjugation pattern: vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven.
The unchanging part of the verb left after removing the -ar/-er/-ir ending (habl-, com-, viv-).

A required word placed before a direct object that is a specific person or pet, with no English equivalent ("Veo a mi hermano," not "Veo mi hermano") — a classic quirk English speakers forget to include.
The six endings attached to a stem to show who is performing the action.
The verb ending must match the subject even when the subject pronoun itself is dropped.

practiceQuestions.question: Conjugate "hablar" for "nosotros":
practiceQuestions.explanation: The -ar ending for nosotros is -amos: hablamos.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sentence correctly includes the personal a?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A specific person as a direct object requires the personal a: "Veo a mi hermano."

practiceQuestions.question: What is the stem (la raíz) of "comer"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Removing the -er ending from comer leaves the stem com-.

practiceQuestions.question: Which verb family does "vivir" belong to?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Vivir ends in -ir, placing it in the -ir verb family.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is the personal a tricky for English speakers?
choices: It has no direct English equivalent
practiceQuestions.explanation: English has no word that functions like the personal a, so learners tend to forget it.

lessons.title: Ser vs. Estar: Two Verbs for "To Be"
lessons.summary: English uses a single verb, "to be," for both permanent traits and temporary conditions. Spanish splits this job between two verbs: **ser** for identity, characteristics, origin, and time, and **estar** for location, temporary states, and ongoing actions. Confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes English-speaking learners make, since swapping them can completely change a sentence's meaning.

keyTerms.definition: "To be" for permanent or inherent traits: identity, profession, origin, physical characteristics, time, and relationships (Soy alta, Es la una, Somos de Texas). Don't confuse with **estar**, which covers temporary states.

"To be" for temporary states, conditions, emotions, location, and ongoing actions (Estoy cansado, El libro está en la mesa). Don't confuse with **ser**: using ser for a location or a temporary feeling is a common beginner error.
A memory trick for when to use estar: Position, Location, Action (in progress), Condition, Emotion — all temporary or situational, unlike ser's permanent traits.
The same adjective changes meaning with the verb: "ser listo" = to be clever/smart (permanent trait), "estar listo" = to be ready (temporary state).
"Ser aburrido" = to be a boring person, "estar aburrido" = to be bored right now — identical words, opposite meaning depending on the verb chosen.
Location always uses estar, even for seemingly permanent locations like "Madrid está en España," which surprises learners who expect ser for something unchanging.
Estar combines with an -ando/-iendo form to describe an action currently in progress ("Estoy comiendo").

practiceQuestions.question: "Mi hermana ___ doctora." (a permanent profession)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Profession is a lasting characteristic, so ser is used.

practiceQuestions.question: "Yo ___ cansado hoy." (a temporary condition)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Being tired is a temporary state, which calls for estar, not ser.

practiceQuestions.question: "Madrid ___ en España." Even though the location seems permanent, Spanish requires:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Location always takes estar, regardless of how permanent that location is.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the difference between "Ella es lista" and "Ella está lista"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ser listo describes an inherent trait (smart); estar listo describes a temporary state (ready).

practiceQuestions.question: Which sentence correctly uses estar to describe an action in progress?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The present progressive combines estar with a gerund (-iendo), not ser.

lessons.title: Irregular Present-Tense Verbs
lessons.summary: Several high-frequency verbs break the regular -ar/-er/-ir patterns. This lesson covers key irregular verbs like **tener**, **ir**, **hacer**, **querer**, and **poder**, along with a grammar quirk that reverses English logic: Spanish uses **tener** ("to have") in idioms where English uses "to be," such as "tener hambre" ("to have hunger" = "to be hungry").

keyTerms.definition: Yo tengo, tú tienes, él tiene... irregular in the "yo" form and stem.
Voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van — highly irregular, not following the -ir pattern at all.
Irregular "yo" form: hago (not "haco").
Stem-changing e→ie: quiero, quieres, quiere...
Stem-changing o→ue: puedo, puedes, puede...

Idioms where Spanish uses "to have" (tener) rather than "to be": "tengo hambre" literally means "I have hunger," not "I am hungry" — the reverse of English logic, and a common source of confusion with ser/estar.
"Going to" + verb, used to express near-future plans (Voy a estudiar).

practiceQuestions.question: Conjugate "ir" for "ellos":
practiceQuestions.explanation: The ellos form of the irregular verb ir is van.

practiceQuestions.question: How do you say "I am hungry" using a tener expression?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Spanish expresses hunger with tener, not ser or estar: "Tengo hambre" literally means "I have hunger."

practiceQuestions.question: What is the irregular "yo" form of "hacer"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hacer's yo form is hago, an irregular spelling change.

practiceQuestions.question: Which verb is stem-changing (e→ie), as in "quiero, quieres, quiere"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Querer changes its stem vowel from e to ie in most present-tense forms.

practiceQuestions.question: "Voy a estudiar" expresses:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ir a + infinitivo describes something the speaker is going to do soon.

lessons.title: Family Vocabulary and Adjective Agreement
lessons.summary: Every Spanish noun carries **grammatical gender**, even objects with no natural gender at all — a category English simply doesn't have. This lesson covers family vocabulary alongside the rule that descriptive adjectives must agree with the noun in both gender and number, unlike invariable English adjectives.

keyTerms.definition: Family vocabulary: el padre/la madre, el hermano/la hermana, los abuelos, el primo/la prima.
Every Spanish noun is either masculine or feminine, even for objects with no natural gender (la mesa, el libro) — a category English doesn't have.
Definite articles that must match the noun's gender and number.
Adjectives must match the noun in both gender and number ("el hermano alto" vs. "la hermana alta" vs. "los hermanos altos"), unlike invariable English adjectives.
Common descriptive adjectives that change their ending to agree with gender.
Possessive adjectives, which agree in number with the thing owned, not with the owner.
Describing a family member's temporary feeling uses estar (Mi hermano está feliz hoy), reinforcing the ser/estar distinction.

practiceQuestions.question: Choose the correctly gendered article: "___ mesa"
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mesa is a feminine noun, so it takes la.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sentence shows correct adjective agreement?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hermanas is feminine plural, so the adjective must also be feminine plural: altas.

practiceQuestions.question: The possessive "mis" agrees with...
practiceQuestions.explanation: Spanish possessives like mi/mis agree in number with the object owned, not the owner's gender.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sentence correctly describes a family member's temporary mood, applying the ser/estar distinction?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A temporary mood uses estar rather than ser.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does Spanish require "el libro" (masculine) even though a book has no natural gender?
choices: All Spanish nouns are grammatically masculine or feminine regardless of meaning
Books are considered male in Hispanic culture
practiceQuestions.explanation: Grammatical gender applies to every noun in Spanish, not just living things.

lessons.title: School, Daily Routine, and Reflexive Verbs
lessons.summary: Many daily-routine actions in Spanish use **reflexive verbs**, where the subject performs the action on itself, marked by -se in the infinitive (levantarse, ducharse). This grammatical category has no exact English structural equivalent, since English rarely needs a built-in reflexive pronoun for routine actions like "getting up."

keyTerms.definition: Verbs where the subject performs the action on itself, marked with -se in the infinitive (levantarse, ducharse, vestirse) — a structural category with no exact English equivalent.

keyTerms.term: me, te, se, nos, os, se
keyTerms.definition: Reflexive pronouns that must match the subject and are placed before the conjugated verb.
To get (oneself) up; "Me levanto a las siete" = "I get up at seven."
To wake (oneself) up vs. to fall asleep — easily confused reflexive pairs with opposite meanings.
School schedule vocabulary: la clase, el recreo, la tarea, el examen.
School subjects: matemáticas, historia, ciencias, educación física, etc.
"Before/after doing something," used to sequence daily routine actions.

practiceQuestions.question: What makes a verb "reflexive" in Spanish?
choices: The subject performs the action on itself
It's only used in the past tense
practiceQuestions.explanation: A reflexive verb marks that the subject and the recipient of the action are the same person.

practiceQuestions.question: Complete: "Yo ___ a las siete." (I get myself up at seven.)
practiceQuestions.explanation: The yo form needs the reflexive pronoun me plus the conjugated verb: me levanto.

practiceQuestions.question: What's the difference between "despertarse" and "dormirse"?
choices: To wake up vs. to fall asleep
practiceQuestions.explanation: Despertarse means to wake up, while dormirse means to fall asleep — opposite actions.

practiceQuestions.question: Which reflexive pronoun matches "nosotros"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nos is the reflexive pronoun used with nosotros.

practiceQuestions.question: "Antes de comer, me lavo las manos" means:
choices: After eating, I wash my hands
Before eating, I wash my hands
While eating, I wash my hands
Instead of eating, I wash my hands
practiceQuestions.explanation: Antes de means "before," so the hand-washing happens before eating.

lessons.title: Food, Meals, and Gustar-Type Verbs
lessons.summary: The verb **gustar** works backward compared to English "to like": the thing being liked is the grammatical subject, and the person doing the liking is an indirect object. This structural quirk — "Me gusta la pizza" literally means "Pizza is pleasing to me" — trips up nearly every English-speaking learner at first.

keyTerms.term: el desayuno / el almuerzo / la cena
keyTerms.definition: Breakfast / lunch / dinner.

A verb that works backward from English "to like": the thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person is an indirect object ("Me gusta la pizza" literally = "Pizza is pleasing to me") — a structural quirk that trips up almost every English-speaking learner.
Singular vs. plural forms of gustar, which must agree with the thing(s) liked, not with the person who likes them.
Indirect object pronouns used with gustar and similar verbs (encantar, interesar, molestar).
La fruta, la verdura, la carne, el pescado, el arroz.
"To love/really please" — grammatically identical to gustar, just expressing a stronger feeling.
Waiter/waitress and "to order" (food) — vocabulary relevant to restaurant conversation.

practiceQuestions.question: How do you correctly say "I like apples" using gustar?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Manzanas is plural, so gustar must agree in the plural form: gustan.

practiceQuestions.question: In "Me gusta el café," what is the grammatical subject of the sentence?
practiceQuestions.explanation: El café is the thing doing the "pleasing," making it the grammatical subject, while me is the indirect object.

practiceQuestions.question: Which indirect object pronoun matches the subject "ellos" (they) when using gustar?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Les is the indirect object pronoun used for ellos/ellas/ustedes.

practiceQuestions.question: What's the difference between gustar and encantar?
choices: Encantar is only used in the past tense
Encantar expresses a stronger liking but works the same grammatically
Gustar is formal and encantar is informal
practiceQuestions.explanation: Encantar follows the same backward structure as gustar but conveys a stronger feeling, like "love" rather than "like."

practiceQuestions.question: Why is "Me gusta la pizza" NOT literally "I like pizza"?
choices: Because the thing liked is the grammatical subject, not the person
Because pizza is a masculine noun
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gustar reverses English sentence logic: the liked item is the subject, and the person is only an indirect object.

lessons.title: The Preterite Tense
lessons.summary: The **preterite** tense describes actions completed at a specific point in the past, with a clear beginning and end. This lesson covers regular preterite endings for all three verb families and a few essential irregular forms, including a quirk where **ir** and **ser** share identical conjugations in this tense.

keyTerms.definition: The past tense used for actions completed at a specific point in time (Ayer comí pizza).
Preterite endings for -ar verbs.
Preterite endings for -er and -ir verbs.

keyTerms.term: ir / ser en pretérito (fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron)
keyTerms.definition: Ir and ser share identical preterite conjugations; context alone tells you which verb is meant — a quirk with no English equivalent.
Irregular preterite stems that don't follow the regular endings pattern.

keyTerms.term: marcadores de tiempo del pretérito (ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, una vez)
keyTerms.definition: Time markers that signal the preterite tense: yesterday, last night, last week, once.

practiceQuestions.question: Conjugate "hablar" in the preterite for "yo":
practiceQuestions.explanation: The preterite yo ending for -ar verbs is -é: hablé.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the preterite "yo" form of "hacer"?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hacer has the irregular preterite stem hic-, giving hice for yo.

practiceQuestions.question: "Fui" could correctly translate to which two different meanings depending on context?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fui is the shared preterite form of both ir (I went) and ser (I was).

practiceQuestions.question: Which time marker signals the preterite tense?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ayer ("yesterday") points to a completed, specific-time action, matching the preterite.

practiceQuestions.question: What kind of actions does the preterite describe?
choices: Actions completed at a specific point in time
practiceQuestions.explanation: The preterite marks a completed action with a clear beginning and end.

lessons.title: The Imperfect Tense
lessons.summary: The **imperfect** tense describes ongoing, habitual, or background actions in the past with no defined endpoint. Unlike the preterite, the imperfect has only three irregular verbs total, making it one of the more regular corners of Spanish grammar.

keyTerms.definition: The past tense used for ongoing, habitual, or background actions with no defined endpoint (Cuando era niño, jugaba mucho).
Imperfect endings for -ar verbs.
Imperfect endings for -er and -ir verbs.

keyTerms.term: verbos irregulares en imperfecto (ser, ir, ver)
keyTerms.definition: Only three verbs are irregular in the imperfect: era (ser), iba (ir), and veía (ver).

keyTerms.term: marcadores de tiempo del imperfecto (siempre, todos los días, de niño/a, frecuentemente, mientras)
keyTerms.definition: Time markers that signal ongoing or habitual past actions: always, every day, as a child, frequently, while.
The imperfect sets the scene: describing weather, time, age, or emotional state in the past ("Era de noche y llovía").

practiceQuestions.question: Conjugate "hablar" in the imperfect for "yo":
practiceQuestions.explanation: The imperfect yo ending for -ar verbs is -aba: hablaba.

practiceQuestions.question: Which three verbs are irregular in the imperfect?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ser, ir, and ver are the only irregular verbs in the imperfect tense.

practiceQuestions.question: Which time marker typically signals the imperfect rather than the preterite?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Todos los días ("every day") signals a habitual, repeated action, which calls for the imperfect.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the imperfect used for?
choices: Ongoing or habitual past actions and background description
practiceQuestions.explanation: The imperfect describes actions without a defined endpoint, including habits and background scenes.

practiceQuestions.question: "Era de noche y llovía" uses the imperfect to:
choices: Set the scene/background of a past situation
practiceQuestions.explanation: The imperfect here paints the background conditions (night, raining) rather than a single completed event.

lessons.title: Preterite vs. Imperfect: Choosing the Right Past Tense
lessons.summary: English has only one simple past tense ("I ate," "I was eating"), but Spanish requires choosing between the **preterite** and the **imperfect** depending on whether an action was a completed, one-time event or an ongoing/habitual background action. This distinction is one of the hardest concepts for English speakers to internalize, since the same verb can carry two different meanings depending on which past tense is chosen.

keyTerms.definition: The core distinction: preterite = a completed action at a specific moment; imperfect = an ongoing, repeated, or background action with no clear end. Don't confuse them — choosing the wrong one changes the sentence's meaning, not just its "flavor."

A common combined use: the imperfect sets an ongoing background scene while the preterite marks the action that interrupted it ("Miraba la tele cuando sonó el teléfono" = "I was watching TV when the phone rang").
The same verb changes meaning by tense: "Conocí a Juan" (preterite) = "I met Juan" (a one-time event), while "Conocía a Juan" (imperfect) = "I knew/used to know Juan" (an ongoing state).

"Supe la verdad" (preterite) = "I found out the truth" (a specific moment), while "Sabía la verdad" (imperfect) = "I knew the truth" (an ongoing state) — the same verb, very different meanings depending on tense.

keyTerms.term: eventos únicos vs. hábitos (single events vs. habits)
keyTerms.definition: A quick test: if "used to" or "was/were -ing" fits naturally in English, the imperfect is likely correct; if it's a one-time completed event, the preterite is likely correct.

keyTerms.term: cambio de significado según el tiempo (meaning shift by tense)
keyTerms.definition: A broader grammar quirk: verbs like conocer, saber, poder, and querer change their English translation depending on whether they're in the preterite or the imperfect.
